title: Variation & Survival Advantage
keyIdea: Living things of the same kind are not exactly alike: they vary in size, colour, shape and more. This is called variation. Some differences give an advantage in a habitat: a dark beetle on dark soil is harder for birds to spot, so it is more likely to survive. Survivors have the young, and young tend to be like their parents, so over many generations the helpful feature becomes more common. A difference that helps in one place can be a problem in another, and animals do not change on purpose.
familyTip: Look at a handful of leaves from one tree, or the people in your family. Talk about how they are the same kind but still differ. Then ask: which difference might help a leaf or an animal in a hot, dry summer, and why?

visual.caption: Does this difference help the living thing survive where it lives? Drag each card to a box, or tap the card and then a box.

items: A pale moth on pale bark
A hare with thick fur in the snow
A cactus with long roots in a dry desert
A pale moth on dark, sooty bark
A bright pink frog on brown leaves with no poison
A thick-furred animal in a hot desert

lab.caption: Flagship lab: measure beetles of one kind, send birds to hunt on dark soil and pale sand, breed the survivors, and match each difference to its advantage.

kid: Look at six beetles of the same kind. One is 11 mm long and one is 15 mm. Some shells are pale and some are dark. Living things of one kind are never exactly the same. This is called variation.
Some differences help. Birds eat beetles they can see. On dark soil a pale beetle stands out, so a bird finds it first. A dark beetle is hard to see, so it is more likely to live.
The beetles that live have the babies. Babies look like their parents. So after many years on dark soil, most beetles are dark.
A difference that helps in one place can hurt in another. On pale sand the dark beetles are easy to see. An animal does not change on purpose. It is born with its features.
adult: Ages 8 to 9. The US standard NGSS 3-LS4-2 asks pupils to use evidence to explain how differences between members of one species can help them survive, find mates and have young. Its own examples are camouflage colours and larger thorns. In England the same idea is built up to in Year 6 Evolution and inheritance. There, pupils learn that young vary and are not identical to their parents, and that adaptation may lead to evolution.

The model has three parts. First, individuals vary: the lab's beetles range from 11 to 15 mm and from very pale to very dark. Second, some differences help in a given place, so those individuals are more likely to survive and breed. Third, young tend to look like their parents, so the helpful feature spreads over the generations. In a year with no birds, no shade is picked out and the mix stays the same. That shows the birds cause the change, not the beetles.

Common mistakes: thinking all members of a species are the same; thinking animals change because they need to or try to, such as a beetle turning dark or a giraffe passing on a stretched neck; thinking one feature is best everywhere; and mixing up survival with strength. Research on how pupils explain natural selection (for example Bishop and Anderson, 1990) finds the need-based idea is the most common slip. In the lab the hunt, the no-birds year and the place cards each test one of these.

practice.prompt: Six beetles of the same kind are measured. What do you expect to find?
choices: They differ a little in size and colour
They are all exactly the same
Only the young ones differ
practice.hint: Think about people in a class. Are any two exactly the same?
practice.explain: Individuals of one kind vary. The lab beetles were 11 to 15 mm long, with shells from very pale to very dark.

practice.prompt: 12 beetles live on dark soil and {p} of them are pale. Birds catch every pale beetle. How many beetles are left?
practice.hint: The pale beetles stand out on dark soil. Take them away from the 12.
practice.explain: 12 − {p} = {=12-p} beetles are left, and none of them are pale, so their young will mostly be dark.

practice.prompt: Each of the {n} surviving beetles has 2 young that look like it. How many young are there?
practice.hint: Each survivor has 2 young. Double the number of survivors.
practice.explain: {n} × 2 = {=2*n} young. Because they look like their parents, the survivors' colour becomes more common.

practice.prompt: On pale sand, which beetles are most likely to survive the birds?
choices: The pale ones
The dark ones
The biggest ones
practice.hint: Which shells would be hard to see against pale sand?
practice.explain: Pale shells match pale sand, so birds spot the dark beetles first. The same difference that helped on dark soil is a problem here.

practice.prompt: Why do dark beetles become more common on dark soil?
choices: More dark ones survive and their young are dark too
The beetles decide to turn dark
The soil paints them dark
practice.hint: Who has the young: the beetles that were caught, or the ones that lived?
practice.explain: Dark beetles were already dark. More of them survive, and their young look like them, so dark becomes common.

choices: Differences between living things of the same kind
When an animal changes on purpose
When all young look exactly like their parents
pool.hint: Think of the six beetles you measured.
pool.explain: Variation means individuals of one kind differ, for example in size or shell colour.

pool.prompt: A rose with sharper thorns is less likely to be eaten. Why does this matter?
choices: It survives to make more seeds
It grows taller
It makes the other roses sharper
pool.hint: What can a plant do if it is not eaten?
pool.explain: A rose that is not eaten lives to make seeds, and its young are likely to have sharp thorns too.

pool.prompt: A giraffe stretches its neck all its life. Are its young born with longer necks because of the stretching?
choices: No, stretching is not passed on
Yes, the stretch is passed on
Only if it is a male
pool.hint: Is a change during an animal's life passed to its young?
pool.explain: Changes during a life are not passed on. Giraffes born with longer necks reach more food, survive and pass that on.

pool.prompt: In a group of 12 moths, {d} are dark and the rest are pale. How many are pale?
pool.hint: Take the dark moths away from the 12.
pool.explain: 12 − {d} = {=12-d} pale moths. The moths vary in colour even though they are one kind.

pool.prompt: Would thick fur help an animal in a hot desert?
choices: No, it would make it too hot
Yes, thick fur always helps
Only if the fur is white
pool.hint: Thick fur keeps heat in. Is that good when it is very hot?
pool.explain: Thick fur keeps heat in, which helps in the Arctic but makes an animal overheat in a hot desert.

pool.prompt: In a year with no birds, what happens to the mix of pale and dark beetles?
choices: It stays about the same
They all turn dark
They all turn pale
pool.hint: If no one is hunting, are pale or dark beetles picked out?
pool.explain: With no birds, no shade is picked out, so the young have the same mix as their parents.

pool.prompt: Peahens choose males with brighter tails. How does a bright tail help a peacock?
choices: He is more likely to find a mate and have chicks
It keeps him warm
It helps him hide from foxes
pool.hint: Who chooses the males, and what for?
pool.explain: A brighter tail makes him more likely to be chosen as a mate, so he has more chicks, and bright tails spread.

pool.prompt: {s} beetles survive the birds. Each one has 3 young. How many young are there?
pool.hint: Multiply the number of survivors by 3.
pool.explain: {s} × 3 = {=3*s} young. Only survivors have young, so their features are passed on.
